Toxicology Chapter 179

Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors

MAOI toxicity is dangerous because it can create a delayed hyperadrenergic crisis, serotonin syndrome, seizures, hyperthermia, hypotension, dysrhythmias, and multiorgan failure.

Board lens: MAOI overdose can look okay early. Toxicity is often delayed 6-12 hours and may be delayed up to 24 hours. Admit/monitor.

Overview

Tintinalli Source Check

FDA-approved MAOIs

Nonselective MAOIsPhenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid are the classic high-risk antidepressants.
MAO-B agentsSelegiline/rasagiline can lose selectivity at high dose or with interactions.
Reversible vs irreversibleTraditional MAOIs bind irreversibly; enzyme recovery can take weeks.

Mechanism and Pharmacokinetics

Tintinalli Source Check
Delayed toxicity: blood levels do not correlate well with clinical toxicity; symptoms can emerge late after ingestion.

Drug and Food Interactions

MAOIs interact with tyramine-rich foods, indirect sympathomimetics, serotonergic drugs, and selected metabolic inhibitors. This is where many board questions live.

Tintinalli Source Check
InteractionClinical PatternBoard Move
Tyramine / indirect sympathomimeticSudden severe hypertension, headache, tachycardiaShort-acting IV BP control
Serotonergic drugClonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermiaStop agents, benzodiazepines, cooling
Insulin/sulfonylureasHypoglycemia riskCheck glucose early
Cimetidine/ciprofloxacin with rasagilineIncreased rasagiline concentrationMedication reconciliation matters

Clinical Features

Tintinalli Source Check
Mild/earlyHeadache, agitation, nausea, palpitations, tremor, tachycardia.
ModerateHyperreflexia, fasciculations, mydriasis, diaphoresis, hypertension, hallucinations.
SevereComa, seizures, hyperthermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, multiorgan failure.

Diagnosis and Differential

MAOI overdose is a clinical diagnosis based on history. Routine urine drug screens do not reliably detect these agents.

Tintinalli Source Check

Treatment

Tintinalli Source Check

Drug Dose Reference

ProblemTreatment ReferenceBoard Caution
HypertensionPhentolamine 2.5-5 mg IV bolus every 10-15 min or infusion 0.2-0.5 mg/min; nitroprusside infusion titratedUse short-acting titratable agents; avoid beta-blocker monotherapy.
HypotensionIV normal saline; direct-acting norepinephrine if vasopressor requiredAvoid indirect-acting agents such as dopamine/ephedrine when possible.
Seizures/agitationLorazepam/diazepam benzodiazepines; phenobarbital if refractoryPhenytoin is generally ineffective in drug-induced seizures.
HyperthermiaBenzodiazepines, active cooling, intubation/paralysis for severe casesAntipyretics do not treat muscle-generated hyperthermia.
Serotonin syndrome overlapStop serotonergic agents; supportive care; consider cyproheptadine enterally in selected casesLook for clonus/hyperreflexia to distinguish from tyramine reaction.

Disposition and Follow-up

Tintinalli Source Check
Disposition: intentional overdoses and accidental ingestions above concerning thresholds require monitored admission. Even asymptomatic patients need at least 24 hours observation.

Key Points

Delayed toxicityOnset often 6-12 h, may be up to 24 h.
Tyramine reactionSevere hypertension after food/indirect sympathomimetics.
Serotonin overlapClonus/hyperreflexia + serotonergic exposure.
No antidoteSupportive care and early complication treatment.
HypertensionPhentolamine or nitroprusside; avoid beta-blocker-only treatment.
HypotensionFluids then direct-acting norepinephrine if needed.
SeizuresBenzodiazepines first; phenytoin is poor for toxicologic seizures.
DispositionMonitor/admit because early normal exam is not reassuring.

Chapter Assessment

A patient on phenelzine develops severe hypertension and headache shortly after aged cheese and decongestant use. Most likely mechanism?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Tyramine/indirect sympathomimetic hyperadrenergic reaction
Correct choice
MAO-A blockade allows tyramine and indirect sympathomimetics to produce catecholamine excess.
B. Pure anticholinergic blockade
Incorrect choice
Anticholinergic toxicity does not explain tyramine-triggered crisis.
C. Opioid withdrawal
Incorrect choice
Withdrawal can cause sympathetic signs but not this classic food/drug interaction.
D. Methemoglobinemia
Incorrect choice
Methemoglobinemia causes cyanosis/hypoxia, not hypertensive crisis.

Important clinical timing feature of MAOI overdose?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Symptoms always peak in 30 minutes
Incorrect choice
MAOI toxicity is characteristically delayed.
B. Toxicity is often delayed 6-12 hours and can be delayed up to 24 hours
Correct choice
Tintinalli emphasizes delayed onset, often 6-12 hours and up to 24 hours.
C. If asymptomatic at 2 hours, discharge
Incorrect choice
This is unsafe. Observation is prolonged.
D. Only chronic therapeutic use causes toxicity
Incorrect choice
Overdose and interactions can both be dangerous.

Which medication should generally be avoided with MAOIs because it may precipitate serotonin syndrome?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Meperidine
Correct choice
Meperidine is a classic serotonergic contraindication with MAOIs.
B. Acetaminophen
Incorrect choice
Acetaminophen is listed among generally safe medications.
C. Nitroglycerin
Incorrect choice
Nitroglycerin may be used for BP/ischemic symptoms.
D. Benzodiazepines
Incorrect choice
Benzodiazepines are useful for agitation/seizures.

Preferred treatment for MAOI-induced seizures?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Benzodiazepines
Correct choice
Benzodiazepines are first-line for MAOI-induced seizures.
B. Phenytoin
Incorrect choice
Phenytoin is generally ineffective for drug-induced seizures.
C. Physostigmine
Incorrect choice
Physostigmine is not indicated.
D. Naloxone
Incorrect choice
Naloxone treats opioids, not MAOI seizures.

Best antihypertensive approach in severe MAOI hypertensive crisis?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Short-acting titratable IV agents such as phentolamine or nitroprusside
Correct choice
Short-acting titratable agents are recommended due to rapid changes and need for careful control.
B. Long-acting oral beta-blocker alone
Incorrect choice
Beta-blockers risk unopposed vasoconstriction and are relatively contraindicated.
C. No therapy; wait for spontaneous resolution
Incorrect choice
Severe crisis needs treatment.
D. High-dose epinephrine
Incorrect choice
Epinephrine worsens adrenergic toxicity.

Hypotension after MAOI overdose should be managed with fluids and, if needed, which vasopressor type is preferred?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Indirect-acting dopamine only
Incorrect choice
Dopamine and other indirect agents should be avoided when possible.
B. Direct-acting norepinephrine
Correct choice
Tintinalli notes direct-acting norepinephrine is preferred when vasopressors are needed.
C. Ephedrine
Incorrect choice
Ephedrine is indirect acting and can be problematic.
D. Tyramine
Incorrect choice
Tyramine is part of the problem, not treatment.

Which finding helps separate serotonin syndrome in an MAOI patient from tyramine reaction alone?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Neuromuscular findings such as clonus/hyperreflexia
Correct choice
Serotonin syndrome has cognitive-behavioral and neuromuscular abnormalities.
B. Hypertension only
Incorrect choice
Hypertension can occur in tyramine reaction or spontaneous crisis.
C. Headache after cheese
Incorrect choice
Food relation favors tyramine reaction.
D. Tachycardia only
Incorrect choice
Tachycardia is nonspecific.

GI decontamination in MAOI overdose is best summarized as:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Activated charcoal may be considered within 1 hour; lavage/WBI generally not useful
Correct choice
Tintinalli supports charcoal within 1 hour but not routine lavage/WBI.
B. Whole bowel irrigation is mandatory for all patients
Incorrect choice
Not recommended routinely.
C. Hemodialysis clears MAOIs effectively
Incorrect choice
MAOIs are highly protein bound/large Vd; dialysis is not useful.
D. Urinary acidification is recommended
Incorrect choice
Urinary acidification is ineffective and may worsen renal complications.

Disposition for intentional MAOI overdose is:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Discharge if normal ECG at 4 hours
Incorrect choice
Delayed toxicity makes this unsafe.
B. Admit to monitored setting/ICU depending severity; asymptomatic patients need at least 24 hours monitoring
Correct choice
This matches Tintinalli disposition.
C. Observe 1 hour only
Incorrect choice
Too short.
D. Outpatient follow-up only
Incorrect choice
Not safe for overdose.

Treatment of severe hyperthermia from MAOI toxicity should prioritize:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Acetaminophen
Incorrect choice
Drug-induced hyperthermia is muscle/activity mediated, not prostaglandin fever.
B. Benzodiazepines, active cooling, and paralysis/intubation when severe
Correct choice
Reduce muscle activity and cool aggressively; severe cases may need airway/paralysis.
C. Aspirin and observation
Incorrect choice
Not adequate.
D. Beta-blocker monotherapy
Incorrect choice
Does not treat hyperthermia and may be harmful.
